subject: Anthropology
title: Taboo
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Taboo.

hook.text: Don't eat pork. Don't say the dead person's name. Don't marry your cousin. Every culture has forbidden zones.

buildup.text: A taboo is a cultural prohibition so strong that violating it brings disgust, punishment, or supernatural danger.

discovery.text: Taboos regulate food, sex, death, and language — the areas where human behavior is most charged with emotion.

twist.text: Mary Douglas showed that taboos mark boundaries between pure and impure, order and disorder in a culture.

climax.text: Taboos reveal what a society most fears. They are invisible fences that guard the cultural order.

punchline.text: What you can't do defines who you are.

quiz.question: According to Mary Douglas, what do taboos mark?
options: Boundaries between purity and pollution in a culture

details.summary: Taboos are culturally prohibited behaviors whose violation provokes strong moral disgust or supernatural punishment. From food restrictions to incest prohibitions, taboos mark the boundaries of acceptable behavior and define what a culture considers most dangerous or sacred.
details.whyItMatters: Taboos reveal what cultures consider most threatening to social order. The intensity of revulsion they provoke shows how deeply cultural norms are internalized — taboo violations feel wrong at a visceral, bodily level.
takeaways: Taboos are culturally prohibited behaviors provoking strong disgust
They mark boundaries between acceptable and dangerous conduct
Taboo violations provoke visceral revulsion, not just disapproval

faq.question: Are some taboos universal across all cultures?
faq.answer: The incest taboo is the closest to universal, though definitions of incest vary. Most cultures have food taboos, death-related taboos, and taboos around bodily functions. The specific content varies enormously, but the category of taboo itself is universal.

faq.question: Why do different cultures have different food taboos?
faq.answer: Ecological, historical, religious, and symbolic factors all play roles. Hindu cow avoidance, Jewish and Islamic pork prohibition, and insect-eating taboos in some Western cultures each have distinct historical explanations. No single theory explains all food taboos.
